new_statements.quote: When a Láadan vowel is written with an accent mark above it, it is a vowel with high tone. English doesn't have any tones, but that will be no problem for you, since you can express it as heavy stress. Think of the way that you distinguish the noun "convert" from the verb "convert" by stressing one of the two syllables. If you pronounce a high-toned Láadan vowel as you would pronounce a strongly-stressed English syllable, you will achieve the same effect as high tone. Because Láadan does not use English stress, this will not be a source of confusion.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Láadan has no word-stress system. Prominence within the word is a lexically specified high tone, written with an acute accent on the vowel (any syllable may carry it; e.g. Lá-a-dan, wáa vs waá). Elgin states explicitly that the language does not use (English-type) stress, and tells English-speaking learners to realise the high-toned vowel as if it were a heavily stressed syllable. Companion lesson text (Elgin, Lessons for Beginners, Lesson One) says the same: high-toned vowel = slightly higher pitch and a bit more emphasis.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Related constraint (Wikipedia, from Elgin's materials): two identical adjacent vowels in a morpheme must differ in tone (máa or maá, never *maa); an epenthetic h separates them across affix boundaries.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; the accent is part of the orthographic/lexical form of each word. Barnhart's primer shows that in transliterating English names the high tone is placed on the English-stressed syllable (Ána, Bétheni), i.e. tone is the sole prominence carrier. Constructed language (Elgin 1982); no dialects.
new_statements.identity_note: Láadan is a constructed language (Suzette Haden Elgin, 1982) with no dialects; the source is the creator's own grammar, which is the only primary description. Glottolog lists no references for laad1235.

sources.citation: Barnhart, Amberwind. 2021-2025. Primer of Láadan: Simple to Advanced Lessons & Workbook, with comments from Suzette Haden Elgin. laadanlanguage.org (499 pp., updated 2025-05-29). Lesson 1 'Pronunciation & Transliteration', p. 1.1.
sources.note: Reproduces Elgin's 1988 paragraph verbatim (high tone = accent; may be rendered as heavy stress; Láadan does not use English stress). Transliteration examples put high tone on the syllable that carries English stress (Ána, Bétheni) 'to simulate the English stress pattern'.
